paras: The attempted lynching of James Henry Harris took place in King and Queen County, Virginia, in the summer of 1895, when a mob threatened a young Black man charged with attempting to assault a six-year-old white girl as he was being taken to jail. The arresting officer, the child's father, turned the would-be lynchers away, and Harris was hanged under a court sentence at King and Queen Courthouse on 23 August 1895. White papers treated the officer's protection of the prisoner as remarkable and praised it in news stories and an editorial.

Harris, nineteen according to the Richmond Times, told the Richmond Dispatch that he was born in Richmond in 1873, had come to the county on a visit in 1892, and had stayed on as a member and Sunday-school teacher at Bethlehem Baptist church. He was charged with an attempt to commit criminal assault upon the six-year-old daughter of the county jailer, a crime the Dispatch dated to early July. According to the Times, the girl's two older brothers reported it to their father after Harris allegedly offered to pay them for silence and threatened to kill them.

The father, a deputy sheriff as well as jailer, made the arrest himself. On the way to the jail he was met by a mob that, in the Times's words, desired to speed vengeance upon the prisoner. He "warded off the would-be lynchers" and told them that as an officer of the law it was his duty to see that the law took its course. The coverage gives no date, place or size for the mob, and no one was reported hurt.

Harris was convicted and sentenced to death, though no report of the trial itself was found. He was hanged in private on 23 August 1895; a large crowd gathered, but only thirty-four people were admitted, and Sheriff Eubank sprang the trap at 12:10. Rev. Charles Morris attended him, and he was buried near the courthouse.

The episode reached print only with the execution, and the coverage found is entirely from white papers. The Richmond Times ran it under "A Father's High Honor," calling Harris "the brute" while praising the jailer, an "old Confederate soldier," for protecting "the villain who sought to ruin his own child." A Richmond wire brief, carried the same day by the Alexandria Gazette, the Roanoke Times and the Raleigh News & Observer, called the arrest "a unique feature of the case"; the Raleigh paper headed it "A Negro Rapist Hanged." A shorter wire naming him ran in the Birmingham Age-Herald as "A Fiend Legally Strangled" and in the Savannah Morning News as "Would-Be Ravisher Hanged."

On 29 August the News & Observer devoted an editorial, "More Than Roman Virtue," to the deputy sheriff, quoting the Atlanta Constitution and the Richmond Dispatch. It called the case "the most remarkable" in the country and said such devotion to duty had never before been recorded in American annals.

The wire brief says Harris confessed his crime, and the Times says he told the crowd he had sinned, but the Dispatch's special from the courthouse says he "did not refer to his crime" and only urged hearers to take warning from his end. The News & Observer editorial placed the hanging "At West Point, Va.," while both Richmond papers, one with a courthouse dateline, put it at King and Queen Courthouse.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of James Henry Harris
bases: A mob threatened violence against Harris while the arresting officer took him to jail and was warded off (A1, A3); no one was hurt, and the one death reported is his legal execution after sentence (A1, A2).

The would-be lynchers sought vengeance for an alleged assault on a child but were turned away by the deputy sheriff, so no one was killed by a mob (A1, A3); Harris died on the gallows under a court sentence carried out by Sheriff Eubank (A1, A2).

The hanging is reported independently by the Times and the Dispatch (A1, A2), but the mob's threat appears only in the Times account and wire briefs of the same text (A1, A3, A4, A5) and in an editorial quoting it (A8); the Dispatch's own report of the hanging does not mention it (A2).

accounts.label: Richmond Times account and wire brief
accounts.gist: The child's father, the deputy sheriff and jailer, arrested Harris and on the way to jail protected him from a mob of would-be lynchers; Harris confessed and was hanged in private.

accounts.label: Richmond Dispatch special from the courthouse
accounts.gist: Describes the hanging and Harris's own life story; says he did not refer to his crime on the scaffold, and does not mention the mob.

accounts.label: Raleigh News & Observer editorial
accounts.gist: Quotes the Atlanta Constitution and the Richmond Dispatch in praise of the deputy sheriff's 'Roman virtue' and places the hanging at West Point.

framing.detail: The Times headlined 'A Father's High Honor' and called Harris 'the brute' and 'the villain', praising the jailer for letting the law take its course rather than the mob.
Out-of-state papers ran short wire briefs under headlines such as 'A Negro Rapist Hanged', 'A Fiend Legally Strangled' and 'Would-Be Ravisher Hanged'.
The News & Observer editorial 'More Than Roman Virtue' held up the officer's refusal to yield to the would-be lynchers as a model of 'stern devotion to public duty'.

versions.value: He confessed his crime / announced that he had sinned
On the scaffold he did not refer to his crime

conflicts.note: The wire says he confessed; the Dispatch's on-the-scene special says only that he urged hearers to take warning from his end. Both agree he spoke of his end as a warning.
The local Richmond reports, including a special datelined at the courthouse, are better evidence than the out-of-state editorial.
